title: The published Gaia20cdd grain grid fits both silicate and graphite after a joint WISE source fit
abstract: We test the source of the WISE 12 um excess of Gaia20cdd and its use to identify warm grains. New joint fits to public AllWISE and unWISE images favour flux at the star over a known red source 5.6 arcsec away. The main unWISE fit gives a target flux of 283 +/- 69 microJy and a red-source flux of 18 +/- 58 microJy after blank-position corrections. Three profile models retain the target signal. We use spatial scatter from 135 blank positions instead of independent-pixel errors. We then update the published spherical-grain grid with a W3 excess of 3.43 +/- 1.09 times the stellar photosphere. An exact amplitude-profile update reproduces 1080 prior joint likelihood values to 4.3e-14. The best silicate fits have chi-square 14.20-14.23, and graphite fits have 12.73-12.78, for 13 measurements and two continuous parameters per fixed size case. The maximum likelihood ratio is only 2.0-2.1. The excess has support, but these fits do not establish a unique carbon composition or few-au radius. Limits include spatial confusion, shared WISE exposures, a finite grain grid, diagonal SPHEREx errors, a top-hat W3 response and the assumption of a stable dust spectrum between 2010 and 2025-2026. Code, source hashes, aggregate results and retrieval instructions are included. Job sci-1107-hp-astronomy-0534dd75bab4; topic astronomy; machine hp; model gpt-6.1-sol.

display.caption: Both materials give low residuals in the published spherical-grain grid with the new W3 constraint. Radius remains conditional on the material. The horizontal reference is the overall minimum plus four, not a calibrated confidence boundary.

Joint source fits retain flux near Gaia20cdd and give little flux at the known red source. Contours use a Gaussian approximation to spatial covariance; bars use spatial errors. The two image products share exposures.
Blank-position histograms and fit-region tests show the effect of spatial noise, background and profile assumptions.
